subject: physics

items.q: Which statement describes the domestic electricity supply in the United Kingdom?
items.correct: An alternating supply of about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz
items.misconception: A direct supply of about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz
items.why: Students meet dc first, with cells, and see that a mains appliance runs smoothly with no visible flickering. A steady effect is read as a steady, one-directional potential difference. A steady effect does not mean a steady direction. The mains potential difference reverses direction 50 times over in every second; appliances are simply too slow to respond to each reversal. Mains electricity is an ac supply.
items.random_wrong: An alternating supply of about 50 V with a frequency of 230 Hz

items.q: What is the difference between a direct and an alternating potential difference?
items.correct: A direct potential difference is always in the same direction; an alternating one repeatedly reverses
items.misconception: A direct potential difference never changes in size; an alternating one changes in size only
items.why: Graphs of ac are often described loosely as 'the voltage changing', and a changing size is easier to picture than a changing direction. The defining feature is the change of direction. A direct potential difference is always in the same direction even if its size varies; an alternating potential difference repeatedly reverses direction.
items.random_wrong: A direct potential difference moves charge round a circuit; an alternating one moves none

items.q: The UK domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. What does this tell you about the supply?
items.correct: The alternating potential difference completes 50 full cycles each second
items.misconception: The potential difference at the socket is 50 volts rather than 230 volts
items.why: Two numbers learned together get swapped, especially when the units are not attached to them in memory. Tie each number to its unit: hertz measures frequency, so 50 Hz is the frequency; volts measure potential difference, so about 230 V is the supply potential difference.
items.random_wrong: The potential difference changes size 50 times a second, in one direction

items.q: The outer covering of a three-core cable is cut back. Which set of colours identifies the three wires correctly?
items.correct: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow stripes
items.misconception: Live blue, neutral brown, earth green and yellow stripes
items.why: Blue is associated with warning and danger in other contexts, and the pair is memorised as 'one brown, one blue' without which is which. Live is brown, neutral is blue. Getting this the wrong way round in a plug puts the supply potential difference on the wrong pin, so learn the pairing exactly as the specification gives it.
items.random_wrong: Live brown, neutral green and yellow stripes, earth blue

items.q: What is the job of the earth wire in a three-core cable?
items.correct: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
items.misconception: It carries unwanted current away from the appliance all the time
items.why: The word 'earth' suggests something being carried away and disposed of, and the wire is described as protective, which sounds like a job it is doing all the time. The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault. Its protection comes from being connected and ready, not from carrying current in normal use.
items.random_wrong: It completes the circuit so that charge can pass round it

items.q: In a mains circuit, what is the job of the neutral wire?
items.correct: It completes the circuit, and is at or close to 0 V
items.misconception: It is the safety wire that stops the case becoming live
items.why: Both wires sit at, or close to, 0 V, so a student who sorts wires by potential alone sees no reason to separate them. Equal potential does not mean equal function. The neutral wire completes the circuit in normal use; the earth wire carries no current in normal use and exists to stop the appliance becoming live.
items.random_wrong: It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply

items.q: A voltmeter is connected between the neutral wire and earth in a mains circuit that is working normally. What reading is expected?
items.correct: About 0 V, because the neutral wire is at or close to earth potential
items.misconception: About 230 V, because the neutral wire is part of the same circuit
items.why: Students correctly know the current is the same in a series loop and wrongly transfer that sameness to potential, which is a difference between two points, not a property carried round the loop. Current is the same all the way round, but potential is not. The live wire is at about 230 V relative to earth and the neutral wire is at, or close to, 0 V; that difference is what drives the current.
items.random_wrong: About 230 V, because the neutral wire carries the supply to earth

items.q: When does the earth wire of an appliance carry a current?
items.correct: Only when there is a fault in the appliance
items.misconception: All the time the appliance is switched on
items.why: The word 'earth' suggests something being carried away and disposed of, and the wire is described as protective, which sounds like a job it is doing all the time. The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault. Its protection comes from being connected and ready, not from carrying current in normal use.
items.random_wrong: Whenever the neutral wire carries a current

items.q: A lamp is plugged into a wall socket but its own switch is open. Which statement about the live wire inside the lamp is correct?
items.correct: It is still at about 230 V relative to earth, so it is still dangerous
items.misconception: It is at 0 V, because the open switch disconnects it from the supply
items.why: 'Off' is treated as 'no electricity anywhere', and students picture the whole circuit going dead rather than only the break at the switch. An open switch stops a current but does not remove the potential difference. The live wire remains connected to the supply and stays at about 230 V relative to earth, so it may still be dangerous.
items.random_wrong: It is safe to touch, as long as the neutral wire is not touched too

items.q: A person standing on damp ground touches a bare live wire. Why is this dangerous?
items.correct: It connects live to earth, so about 230 V drives a current through them
items.misconception: It is only dangerous if the neutral wire is touched at the same time
items.why: Circuit diagrams show a loop from live to neutral, so students look for that loop and forget that the ground is itself at 0 V and completes a path. Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. Standing on the ground already puts a person at earth potential, so touching the live wire alone puts about 230 V across them.
items.random_wrong: It is only dangerous if the appliance is switched on at the wall

items.q: Inside a metal-cased heater the live wire works loose and touches the metal case. The case is connected to the earth wire. What happens?
items.correct: A large current passes in the earth wire, as live is now joined to earth
items.misconception: Nothing changes, because the earth wire already carries a current anyway
items.why: The word 'earth' suggests something being carried away and disposed of, and the wire is described as protective, which sounds like a job it is doing all the time. The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault. Its protection comes from being connected and ready, not from carrying current in normal use.
items.random_wrong: The neutral wire carries the fault current, since it is also at 0 V

items.q: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. What does three-core cable contain?
items.correct: Three separately insulated wires: live, neutral and earth
items.misconception: Three wires that all carry a current when the appliance works
items.why: Three wires are visible in the cable and all three are connected to pins in the plug, so all three look equally involved in normal operation. Three-core cable contains three wires, but only two of them form the working circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire and only carries a current if there is a fault.
items.random_wrong: Three layers of insulation, to make the appliance safer to use

items.q: Why is the insulation covering each wire inside a mains cable colour coded?
items.correct: So that each wire can be quickly identified when a plug is wired
items.misconception: So that each wire is allowed to carry a different size of current
items.why: Three wires are visible in the cable and all three are connected to pins in the plug, so all three look equally involved in normal operation. Three-core cable contains three wires, but only two of them form the working circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire and only carries a current if there is a fault.
items.random_wrong: So that the earth wire can be seen while it is carrying a current

items.q: A plug is wired incorrectly, and the brown wire is connected to the earth pin. What is the immediate danger?
items.correct: The earth pin, and any metal case joined to it, is now at about 230 V
items.misconception: There is no danger, because the brown wire is the neutral wire anyway
items.why: Blue is associated with warning and danger in other contexts, and the pair is memorised as 'one brown, one blue' without which is which. Live is brown, neutral is blue. Getting this the wrong way round in a plug puts the supply potential difference on the wrong pin, so learn the pairing exactly as the specification gives it.
items.random_wrong: There is no danger, because the earth wire is always held at 0 V

items.q: A student says that a cell and a mains socket both supply an alternating potential difference. What is wrong with this?
items.correct: A cell supplies a direct potential difference, in one direction only
items.misconception: Nothing is wrong: both reverse, which is why no charge moves at all
items.why: Students equate 'useful electricity' with charge travelling all the way round a loop, so a back-and-forth motion looks like it achieves nothing. Energy transfer does not depend on charge making a one-way journey. Charge moving backwards and forwards through a component still transfers energy, which is why mains appliances work on an ac supply.
items.random_wrong: Nothing is wrong: both change in size, and that is what alternating means

items.q: In a mains circuit that is working normally, how does the potential of the neutral wire compare with earth?
items.correct: It is at, or close to, earth potential, which is 0 V
items.misconception: It is at about 230 V, the same as the live wire is
items.why: Students correctly know the current is the same in a series loop and wrongly transfer that sameness to potential, which is a difference between two points, not a property carried round the loop. Current is the same all the way round, but potential is not. The live wire is at about 230 V relative to earth and the neutral wire is at, or close to, 0 V; that difference is what drives the current.
items.random_wrong: It is at exactly 0 V at all times, with no exception

items.q: Is the neutral wire always at exactly 0 V?
items.correct: It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V) – close to zero rather than guaranteed to be exactly zero.
items.misconception: The neutral wire is exactly 0 V at all times, so it is completely safe to touch in any circumstances.
items.why: '0 V' is remembered as an exact figure, and the wording 'at, or close to' is dropped when the fact is compressed for revision. The specification says the neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). Keep the phrase 'or close to': mains wiring is never treated as safe to touch on the strength of a nominal zero.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the earth pin or earth wire of an appliance ever be at a dangerous potential?
items.correct: Yes, if it is wrongly connected to the live wire, it is raised to about 230 V like any other conductor joined to live.
items.misconception: The earth wire is at 0 V whatever is done to it, so anything connected to the earth pin must be safe.
items.why: 'The earth wire is at 0 V' is memorised as a permanent property of the wire rather than as a description of a correctly wired circuit. The earth wire is at 0 V because it is connected to earth in a correctly wired appliance. Connect it instead to the live wire and it rises to about 230 V, which makes the earth pin and any metal case dangerous.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.3 Domestic uses and safety
